subject: Abundance estimates of populations with multiple species

messages.author: a94bf563bce55f38
messages.subject: Abundance estimates of populations with multiple species
parts:
Dear distance group,

If I have line transect data the has records for more than species, am I able to make abundance estimates for the general population? I am trying to compare total species numbers (all animals), for a given transect, between two years. I could run distance abundance estimation for each species in turn, and then add them up. But I wondered if it was feasible to do this at a cross-species population level.

Thanks

Anthony

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Abundance estimates of populations with multiple species
parts:
Anthony

Several answers to this question, ranging from simple (and perhaps incorrect) to more complex:

  • if you have species recorded at the observation level of your data, you could use Distance and simply ignore the species field.  This would pool data across species producing an abundance estimate.  However, such an analysis would assume detection probability does not differ between species.
  • You could employ the MCDS (multiple covariate distance sampling) engine and use species as a covariate in the detection function and ask for a global density estimate.  That would produce distinct detection functions for multiple species and the density/abundance estimates produced would take the differing detection functions into account.
  • A word of caution however.  I'm not sure how far you could extend the inference about year-to-year abundance differences when using information from a single transect.  I'm not certain what you meant by 'for a given transect.'

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Abundance estimates of populations with multiple species
parts:
Hi,

Just thought I would mention that I read an article (can't seem to find it now) where multiple species were surveyed, and total animal abundance was of interest. Instead of using species as a covariate, they used expected body mass. All individuals of some (small) species had the same expected body mass, in other cases I think they used different values for e.g. juveniles and adults. The advantage is that this requires only one extra model parameter (a continuous covariate), rather than one parameter for each species after the first one. This would assume that differences in detectability as a function of distance across species are attributable to differences in size.

Eric

messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Abundance estimates of populations with multiple species
parts: Hang on a minute.  "Size" is being used in two contexts in this thread.  There is individual body size (perhaps serving as a surrogate of species, under the assumption that detectability is a function of body size rather than behaviour).  There is group size (number of individuals in a detected cluster) that may influence detectability (under the assumption that larger groups are more easily detected than small groups at large distances).

Just thought I would mention that I read an article (can't seem to find it now) where multiple species were surveyed, and total animal abundance was of interest. Instead of using species as a covariate, they used expected body mass. All individuals of some (small) species had the same expected body mass, in other cases I think they used different values for e.g. juveniles and adults. The advantage is that this requires only one extra model parameter (a continuous covariate), rather than one parameter for each species after the first one. This would assume that differences in detectability as a function of distance across species are attributable to differences in size.

On Tue, 26 Feb 2019 at 17:58, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
Anthony

Several answers to this question, ranging from simple (and perhaps incorrect) to more complex:

  • if you have species recorded at the observation level of your data, you could use Distance and simply ignore the species field.  This would pool data across species producing an abundance estimate.  However, such an analysis would assume detection probability does not differ between species. 
Ok. That's probably interesting to get a rough idea, but I'd like to be more accurate. So I might write do this and compare it for a detection for each species, and compare the two approaches. Will be interesting. 
  • You could employ the MCDS (multiple covariate distance sampling) engine and use species as a covariate in the detection function and ask for a global density estimate.  That would produce distinct detection functions for multiple species and the density/abundance estimates produced would take the differing detection functions into account.

I'm using the r package, and I'm not sure how to do this. Is this a feature that is available in the Distance library for r?
  • A word of caution however.  I'm not sure how far you could extend the inference about year-to-year abundance differences when using information from a single transect.  I'm not certain what you meant by 'for a given transect.'
It is a single transect, but has been surveyed many times throughout the year. I have other transects within the same region, that have also been surveyed multiple times. But I thought I'd start with one transect initially.
